title: Uisang goes on
hookLine: Wonhyo turns back; his friend Uisang goes on to China and brings back Huayan
last: IT WAS SWEET IN THE DARK.

cards: Morning, outside the tomb. Two friends stand on the road with their bundles. One of them has just had the night of his life.
Wonhyo says he doesn't need to go to China anymore: if the mind makes everything, there's nothing over there he can't find right here. He turns around and walks home.
The other friend, Uisang, listens, nods, and picks up his bundle. He keeps walking toward the sea. No quarrel.

teach.b: Uisang crossed to China and studied with the teacher Zhiyan, in the school called Huayan, named for the Flower Garland Sutra. That name came up earlier, on the list of Chinese schools.
Huayan pictures the universe as a net of jewels, where every jewel reflects every other one. Nothing stands alone; each thing holds the whole.

teach.h: A NET OF JEWELS, A SEAL-SHAPED POEM.
teach.b: Uisang packed that teaching into a short poem, written in a winding pattern like a seal, so the reader's eye follows a path that folds back on itself. One line says, in plain terms, in one is all, and in many is one.
Back in Korea he founded temples and taught students, and Huayan, called Hwaeom in Korean, took root. An old Chinese life of Uisang adds a story.
Shanmiao, Seonmyo in Korean, was a young woman in China who loved him. When he sailed home, she leapt into the sea and became a dragon to guard his ship, and later a great rock to protect his temple.
Wonhyo never went to China. He stayed, wrote commentaries, and later, the stories say, left the monk's life to walk among villagers, singing and teaching them the Buddha's name.
One friend took the long road out; one took the short road in. Korean Buddhist tradition honors both.
There's an echo of Huayan in that: two very different paths, each holding something of the other.

how: Korean Buddhists honor Uisang as the founder of Hwaeom (Huayan) in Korea, and his seal-shaped poem on the Dharma realm is still recited and studied in Korean temples.

games.q: you're Uisang. your friend has just turned back, saying everything is mind and China is unnecessary. what do you do?
o: wish him well and keep walking.
games.why: Uisang goes on to China, studies Huayan, and brings it home. neither friend is called wrong.

practice: Bring to mind someone you started out beside who went a different way: another city, another kind of work, another pace.
Picture them on their road and you on yours, let any urge to call one road the right one rest, and wish them well, the way Uisang and Wonhyo parted without a quarrel.

wordCard.voice: Huayan. The school Uisang studied in China and carried home to Korea: a universe where every jewel reflects every other jewel.

carryVoice: Your line: two friends, two paths. Neither road was the wrong one. Day nine hundred twenty-one.
